record.paper_title: Infrared tip-tilt sensing: on-sky experience, lessons learned and unsolved problems
record.context_brief: Focus and low-order sensing from PSF images
record.original_question: How can an infrared tip-tilt sensor measure focus and other low-order aberrations from a well-sampled point-spread function in real observing conditions, without requiring a second expensive near-infrared camera, when the same image elongations can also be caused by wind-shake, anisoplanatism for off-axis guide stars, laser-guide-star aberrations, calibration errors, or telescope phasing errors? Any solution must distinguish the intentionally introduced low-order signal, such as in a focal-plane wavefront-sensing method, from these confounding effects and operate with finer point-spread-function sampling than simple spot-displacement estimation.

evidence.quote: In addition to tip-tilt measurements, focus measurements at a lower bandwidth are needed to track the changes in the sodium altitude, and some systems also measure quasi-static aberrations induced by LGS elongation. 1 A number of solutions to avoid the need for second expensive NIR camera have been proposed or implemented: 1. Use a visible light focus sensor operating on the same star as a visible light TTS. This solution, implemented on GeMS and on Keck I, requires a suﬃciently bright gude star in the visible, which partially negates the beneﬁts of a NIR TTS. 2. Use a 2 × 2 SH WFS to measure tip-tilt and focus, as implemented in IRLOS. 3. Use the pixel intensities in a well sampled spot to deduce low-order aberrations.

This technique has been “tested” in simulations and on test benches without atmospheric turbulence. However, there are multiple real-life eﬀects which also elongate the image including wind-shake, anisoplanatic eﬀect (for oﬀ-axis guide stars), so-called LGS aberrations,28 calibration errors and telescope phasing errors (for segmented telescopes). These risks need to be retired or mitigated. A possible solution would be to add dynamic rather than static aberrations. In addition, the use of LIFT requires the PSF to be sampled much more ﬁnely than what is required to estimate the spot displacement.

There are still a number of unsolved research problems and these are listed here: – Measuring focus and other low-order terms from PSF in real-life (e.g., in the presence of wind-shake, oﬀ-axis elongation, quasi-static aberrations) .

artifact.category_tag: Focal-plane wavefront sensing in adaptive optics
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of robustly extracting focus and other low-order aberrations from a well-sampled science-channel PSF in the presence of wind-shake, off-axis anisoplanatism, LGS aberrations, calibration errors, and telescope-phasing errors is repeatedly listed as an unsolved research problem in recent adaptive-optics literature on infrared tip-tilt sensing and focal-plane sensing (e.g., LIFT-based approaches). Methods such as LIFT have been demonstrated only in simulation and on turbulence-free benches; no peer-reviewed on-sky demonstration disentangling all of the listed confounders has been reported as of the search date.

status_evidence.title: LIFT, a focal-plane wavefront sensor for direct phase retrieval
status_evidence.snippet: LIFT is demonstrated in numerical simulations and laboratory bench tests; on-sky robustness to wind-shake, anisoplanatism and LGS aberrations is identified as future work.
status_evidence.claim: Focal-plane low-order sensing methods of the LIFT type have not been validated on-sky against the listed confounding effects.

status_evidence.title: Infrared tip-tilt sensing: on-sky experience, lessons learned and unsolved problems (arXiv:2201.05747)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists measuring focus and low-order terms from the PSF in real-life conditions as an unsolved research problem.
status_evidence.claim: The community survey explicitly classifies this problem as unsolved.
